course_description:
This course introduces students to the ethical dimensions of computing practice, the responsibilities of computing professionals and the critical role of responsible decision-making. Through a case study centred approach, students will explore how everyday design and development decisions can lead to profound social, legal and ethical consequences. Topics include professional codes of conduct, frameworks for ethical decision-making, bias and inclusion, cybersecurity and privacy, sustainability and the ethical challenges of emerging technologies. Students will gain the tools to anticipate the consequences of technological choices beyond mere legal compliance, understand relevant Australian laws and global standards. Students will develop the moral sensitivity and principled reasoning needed for responsible computing.

This course treats all external sources of information (including textbooks, academic articles, developer forums, online tutorials, and generative AI) as pieces of a wider knowledge ecosystem. You are permitted to engage with these diverse forms of cognitive support to help solve complex problems. However, you will be assessed on your ability to critically select, evaluate, and validate these inputs. You retain full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of your decisions. If you choose not to use AI tools, alternative information pathways are fully supported and will not disadvantage you.

The course places particular emphasis on responsible inquiry and judgement. You will work with diverse forms of knowledge, which may include academic research, policy, technical documentation, practitioner and community knowledge, public data, crowdsourced resources and generative systems. You will be expected to determine what knowledge is needed, evaluate what different sources can and cannot contribute, integrate evidence carefully, make uncertainty visible and remain accountable for the conclusions and recommendations you produce.

learning_outcomes.description: Describe the foundation principles and regulatory frameworks that guide and govern professional practice in computing, including relevant codes of conduct and Australian laws pertaining to technology.
Apply ethical decision-making frameworks to anticipate the social, environmental and ethical impact of technological products and development processes.
Explain legal & ethical responsibilities associated with issues related to privacy, security, diversity, inclusion and systems reliability in computing practice.
Identify and critically reflect on personal biases and their potential influence on technological design, development and deployment.

assessment_details.due_date: Proposal (non-graded formative) 21/08/2026 5:00 pm Case Study Report (graded with Interview) 16/10/2026 5:00 pm Oral Interview (graded with Report) 27/10/2026 11:00 am This is a sequence comprising three assessments: a non-graded Proposal to confirm the appropriateness of your case study; a Case Study Report and an Oral Interview (both combined in grading).
assessment_details.task_description: Analyse a computing technology case with respect to the ethical topics covered in this course. Your case study will apply ethical frameworks and principles to a sociotechnical system, evaluating it with respect to, e.g. professional codes of ethics, bias and fairness, accessibility, consent, transparency, privacy, security, relevant legal frameworks and governance. This is a sequence comprising three assessments: a non-graded proposal to confirm the appropriateness of your case study, a case study report and an oral interview. The proposal is a non-graded formative submission that can provide feedback to students before the census date. Students will get feedback on their proposal and learn whether it is appropriate for the course as is, or would be better to revise. Your grade for this assessment is based on your case study report and the oral interview combined. These are not graded separately and your oral interview forms the secure component in this assessment. To be clear, students need to pass (satisfactory) the interview otherwise their grade for this assessment item will be capped at a 3. Details will be provided as part of the assessment brief. In accordance with UQ Assessment Policy, your oral interview will be recorded. assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
See the brief for submission instructions.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 7 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Note the interview component of this assessment is a scheduled in-person recorded secure assessment in Week 13. Extensions are limited to 7 days to ensure students can receive feedback on their proposal before the census date, feedback on their report with sufficient time to incorporate into their oral interview in Week 13, and can receive feedback on their overall Case Study in time to prepare for their Final Examination, with the examination period starting the following week.
Students with approved absences may be offered one rescheduled session. If they do not attend the rescheduled session, they will receive a mark of zero.
Late submission
You will receive a mark of 0 if this assessment is submitted late .
Note the interview component of this assessment is a scheduled in-person recorded secure assessment in Week 13. Late submissions for this component will not be possible without an approved extension. Consistent with industry practice around presentations to clients/industry partners, no late submissions will be accepted and a 100% late penalty applies.
This has been approved by the Associate Dean (Academic)
